## Step 1: Examine reads

Reads are linked into `raw_data/`.
```{r}
#cd ~/mb5370-workshops/raw_data

## symbolic link to rae reads file in the raw_data folder

## using ls to make sure the link is correct for the raw data 

#zcat raw_data/raw_reads.fastq.gz | head -n 40000 | bioawk -c fastx '{print $name,length($seq)}' > read_lengths.txt

#lines underneath explain the code 
# Unzips the raw data and sends the data to standard output
##zcat raw_data/raw_reads.fastq.gz \
# This is a pipe. It sends output from the previous command as input to the next command
  ##| \
# Here we select only the top 40k lines in the file. This equates to 10k reads. It should be plenty to get some stats
 ## head -n 40000 | \
# This is a small bioawk program. It prints the name of each sequence followed by its length
  ##bioawk -c fastx '{print $name,length($seq)}' \
# Send outputs to a file called read_lengths.txt
##  > read_lengths.txt

#making a graph to visualise the data 
library(tidyverse)

rl_data <- read_tsv("read_lengths.txt",col_names = c("id","length"), show_col_types = FALSE)

ggplot(rl_data, aes(x=length/1000)) + 
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 2) +
  xlab("Read Length Kb") + ylab("Number of Reads")

#Figure 1: Histogram of read lengths in the mock nanopore sequencing dataset

# calculating read N50 
total_len <- sum(rl_data$length)

rl_data |> 
  arrange(desc(length)) |> 
  mutate(cumsum = cumsum(length)) |> 
  filter(cumsum>total_len/2) |> 
  head(n=1)



```

## Step 2: Assembly

Commands run in `flye_metagenome/`.

```{r}
#Step 2
#running the batch file 
#sbatch run_flye.sh 
#tail -f slurm-XXX.out to monitor job output 
#it took ~13 minutes 
#3.1 - the largest contig from the bandage is 4,681,066 bp long - edge_42 - contig 42
#3.2 - more adbundant of a species - more DNA to sequence so you will get a more complete genome sequence - so the largest DNA sequence - so the same species as from 3.1 
#3.3 - the largest is vibrio alfacsensis and the 2nd largest is likely to be a different species as it is a complete genome 
#creating a plain text and pasting this - to calculate GC content and size 
# Bioawk script for calculating gc and printing name,length,GC
BEGIN {
    OFS="\t"
}

{
    l=length($seq)
    ngc=gsub("[cgCG]","",$seq)
    nat=gsub("[taTA]","",$seq)
    print $name,l,ngc/(ngc+nat)
}

#saving as gc.awk 
# cd ~/mb5370-workshops
#cat /pvol/data/mg/refs/*.fna | bioawk -c fastx -f gc.awk
#^ testing the awk program to print GC content and contig lengths for chromosomes for all the files in -> ls /pvol/data/mg/refs/*.fna
# CP003591.1      4681111 0.584631 / (chromasome) (contig length) (GC Concent %)
#GC (the amino acids - looking at a specific bond - helps identify specific sequence because GC bonds are less abundant )

```


## Step 3: Basic assembly QC

Commands run in `assembly_check/`.

```{r}
#cat ../flye_metagenome/mock/assembly.fasta | bioawk -c fastx -f ../gc.awk
#^ using gc.awk to print GC and lengths for the assembly 

#sending the outputs into a file 
#cat ../flye_metagenome/mock/assembly.fasta | bioawk -c fastx -f ../gc.awk > assembly.gc.tsv

#making a graph - reading info first 
gc <- read_tsv("assembly_check/assembly.gc.tsv",col_names = c("#seq_name","length","GC"))
info <- read_tsv("flye_metagenome/mock/assembly_info.txt")

#joining the two dataframes because they both include #seq_name 
gc_info <- info |> 
  left_join(gc)

#drawing a histogram by GC content 
gc_info |> 
  ggplot(aes(x=GC)) + geom_histogram() + ylab("Number of contigs")

#Figure 2: Histogram of GC content values for assembled contigs in a flye assembly of the mock community dataset.

#filtering the data - renoving contigs with unrealistically high GC content and very high coverage depth (prob repeats)
gc_info |> 
  filter(GC<0.8) |> 
  filter(cov.<25) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x=GC,y=cov.)) + geom_point(aes(size=length)) + ylab("Coverage depth")
#Figure 3: Coverage and GC content of assembled contigs in the mock community assembly. Contig lengths are shown through point size.

#3.4 - the cluster around GC ~0.65 and coverage around 5 to 10 belongs to a species that could be contaminit or plasmid DNA as they are not full circular DNA - so not a specific bacteria - really tiny fragments 

# adding labels to the contigs/dots 
#library(ggrepel)
library(ggrepel)
gc_info |> 
  filter(GC<0.8) |> 
  filter(cov.<25) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x=GC,y=cov.)) + geom_point(aes(size=length)) + geom_label_repel(aes(label=`#seq_name`))
#Figure 4: Coverage and GC content of assembled contigs in the mock community assembly. Contig lengths are shown through point size. Only contigs with less than 25x coverage and less than 80% GC content are shown.

#calculate the total length of our reference sequences. This command builds on one we ran earlier to list the size and GC content of reference chromosomes, but this time we have added another very simple awk program to take the sum of the second column.
#cat /pvol/data/mg/refs/*.fna | bioawk -c fastx -f gc.awk | awk '{sum+=$2}END{print sum}'

#3.5 - total length of the assembly by taking the sym of the contig lengths column 
contig_sum <- sum(gc_info$length)
contig_sum
#sum = 18326991
#proportion of reference sequence = contig sum/total length 
prop <- contig_sum/total_len
prop
#proportion of the reference sequence is 12.3% 
```
